question: How are enterprises running long-lived AI agents in production?

plan.summary: I will look at where long-lived agents run today, how teams keep their state through failures and waits, what it costs to keep them available, and what operators say goes wrong.
subquestions: Which hosting models do enterprises use for long-lived AI agents, and what are their documented limits?
How do teams preserve agent state across crashes, deployments and multi-day waits for human input?
What does idle time cost on current agent platforms, and which ones scale to zero?
What failure modes do operators report most often for long-running agents in production?

research.subquestion: Which hosting models do enterprises use for long-lived AI agents, and what are their documented limits?
research.findings:
- Managed agent runtimes give each session an isolated sandbox with its own filesystem and an idle timeout after which compute is released; the documented range on one major platform is 2 minutes to 4 hours, default 15 minutes (reviewed November 2026). ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/hosted-agents?utm_source=openai))
- Function-style hosts cap a single invocation at minutes, so teams split agent work into short steps and move the long-lived part into an orchestrator. ([docs.aws.amazon.com](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html?utm_source=openai))
- Container platforms with scale-to-zero remove the time cap but add cold starts of several seconds; operators report 4 to 8 seconds as typical for Python agents with large dependency trees. ([cloud.google.com](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/tips/general?utm_source=openai))
- Kubernetes remains common where teams already run it, usually with an event-driven autoscaler in front of a worker pool, at the price of owning capacity planning. ([keda.sh](https://keda.sh/docs/2.21/scalers/temporal/?utm_source=openai))
- Sources disagree on whether session-based sandboxes or shared worker pools are cheaper at steady load; the answer depends on how bursty the traffic is.

research.subquestion: How do teams preserve agent state across crashes, deployments and multi-day waits for human input?
research.findings:
- Durable execution engines record each completed step and replay the code after a failure, so a model call that already returned is not paid for twice. ([docs.temporal.io](https://docs.temporal.io/evaluate/understanding-temporal?utm_source=openai))
- Checkpoint-based frameworks persist a snapshot between steps; on recovery they restart the current step from its beginning, which the framework authors describe as persistence, not replay. ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/long-running-agent-resilience?utm_source=openai))
- For waits on people, the common pattern is to hold the wait in the orchestrator, release the compute, and resume on a signal or a callback. ([docs.temporal.io](https://docs.temporal.io/develop/python/message-passing?utm_source=openai))
- Version skew during deployments is a recurring problem: in-flight runs must keep executing against the code they started with. ([docs.temporal.io](https://docs.temporal.io/production-deployment/worker-deployments/worker-versioning?utm_source=openai))

research.subquestion: What does idle time cost on current agent platforms, and which ones scale to zero?
research.findings:
- Session-based agent hosting bills per vCPU-hour and GiB-hour only while a session is active; list price in US regions is about $0.10 per vCPU-hour as of November 2026. ([azure.microsoft.com](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/foundry-agent-service/?utm_source=openai))
- An always-on worker of the same size costs roughly $90 a month before any work is done, which is why teams with spiky agent traffic look for scale-to-zero. ([azure.microsoft.com](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/virtual-machines/linux/?utm_source=openai))
- Scale-to-zero only pays off if something outside the compute can wake it; platforms differ on whether timers and retries count as wake events. ([docs.temporal.io](https://docs.temporal.io/serverless-workers?utm_source=openai))

research.subquestion: What failure modes do operators report most often for long-running agents in production?
research.findings:
- Lost work after a restart is the most cited problem: an agent halfway through a task starts over, repeating model calls and tool side effects. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657?utm_source=openai))
- Rate limits and transient model errors account for a large share of failed runs when retries are left to the model SDK. ([platform.openai.com](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/rate-limits?utm_source=openai))
- Waits for approval that outlive the process holding them: the approval arrives and nothing is listening. ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/manage-hosted-sessions?utm_source=openai))
- Operators also report weak visibility: knowing which step ran where, and why it was retried, usually needs custom tracing. ([opentelemetry.io](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/?utm_source=openai))

report:
# Running long-lived AI agents in production

Enterprises are converging on a split: agent code runs on compute that can be released when idle, and a durable orchestrator outside that compute holds the state and decides when to bring it back. The teams that report the fewest incidents treat waits, retries and deployments as orchestration problems, not as agent problems.

## Where the agents run

Managed agent runtimes now give each session an isolated sandbox and release it after an idle timeout, documented at 2 minutes to 4 hours on one major platform ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/hosted-agents?utm_source=openai)). Function-style hosts cap a single invocation at minutes, so long work is cut into steps ([docs.aws.amazon.com](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html?utm_source=openai)). Cold starts of 4 to 8 seconds are typical for Python agents ([cloud.google.com](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/tips/general?utm_source=openai)).

## How state survives

Durable execution records each completed step and replays the code after a failure, so finished model calls are not repeated ([docs.temporal.io](https://docs.temporal.io/evaluate/understanding-temporal?utm_source=openai)). Checkpointing restarts the current step from its beginning, which its own documentation describes as persistence, not replay ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/long-running-agent-resilience?utm_source=openai)). Waits on people are held in the orchestrator while compute is released ([docs.temporal.io](https://docs.temporal.io/develop/python/message-passing?utm_source=openai)).

## What idle time costs

Session-based hosting bills only while a session is active, about $0.10 per vCPU-hour in US regions ([azure.microsoft.com](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/foundry-agent-service/?utm_source=openai)). Scale-to-zero pays off only if timers and retries can wake the compute ([docs.temporal.io](https://docs.temporal.io/serverless-workers?utm_source=openai)).

## What goes wrong

The most cited failures are work lost on restart ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657?utm_source=openai)), rate limits handled by SDK retries, and approvals that arrive when nothing is listening ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/manage-hosted-sessions?utm_source=openai)).

## Open questions

- How do per-session sandboxes compare in cost with shared worker pools at steady load?
- Which platforms treat a timer or a retry as a wake event without extra components?
- How much of the reported cold start is dependency import, and can it be cut?
follow_up:
**Update, one minute later.** Nothing material changed on the three open questions. One new data point: a platform note published this week confirms that session idle timers are reset only by inbound requests, so a timer or a retry needs an outside party to wake the compute ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/manage-hosted-sessions?utm_source=openai)).

Next actions:

1. Measure cold start for the current agent image and split it into platform time and import time.
2. Price one week of real traffic both ways: per-session sandboxes against a two-node worker pool.
3. Re-run this brief after the next platform release notes.
